days.title: What is Technical Communication?
days.summary: Daily speech topic for Day 1 on Technical Communication fundamentals.
days.content:
English Initiative - Phase 3 | Week 1 | Page 2
 DAY 1
What is Technical Communication?
Source: Definition, Features & Types of Technical Communication
Q1. What does the word “Communication” mean, and how is it defined?
Answer (from the study material):
Communication is derived from the Latin word communicare, which means “to share”. According to
William Summer and Charles Newman, “Communication is the act of sharing information, ideas,
opinions, and feelings between a sender and a receiver.”
Simple Explanation (for your understanding):
In simple words, communication only happens when something (information, an idea, an opinion or a
feeling) actually travels from one person, the sender, to another person, the receiver. If nothing is
shared or understood, real communication has not happened.
Q2. What are the main features of Technical Communication?
Answer (from the study material):
Technical Communication has: (1) Audience – a specific audience in mind, based on age, educational
background, social position, etc. (2) Objective – a specific goal to communicate, i.e. to inform, instruct
or persuade the audience. (3) Language – formal language is used; no dialects or slangs; technical
words are used, and their number depends on the audience’s technical exposure. (4) Format –
information is presented in a specific order; reports are long, letters are short. (5) Style – professional,
which means avoiding flowery and emotional words, and staying error-free in grammar, spelling and
punctuation. (6) Visual aids – relevant graphs, charts and pictures are used.
Simple Explanation (for your understanding):
Unlike casual conversation, technical communication is always planned. Before you write or speak, you
already know who you are talking to, what you want them to do (know something, do something, or
agree with something), and you keep the language formal, correct and supported with visuals wherever
needed.
Q3. What are the types of Technical Communication?
Answer (from the study material):
Technical Communication is of two types: Internal – communication inside one organization, mainly
through oral means such as intercom, meetings, conversations and presentations. External –
communication between two organizations, mainly through written means such as emails, press
releases, advertisements, brochures and reports.
Simple Explanation (for your understanding):
Think of Internal communication as talk that stays inside your own college or company, usually spoken.
External communication goes outside, to another organization or the public, and is usually written down
so there is a record of it.

days.title: General vs Technical Communication, Role & Purpose
days.summary: Daily speech topic for Day 2 on Technical Communication fundamentals.
days.content:
English Initiative - Phase 3 | Week 1 | Page 3
 DAY 2
General vs Technical Communication, and Its Role &
Purpose
Source: Difference between General & Technical Communication; Role and Purpose of Technical
Communication
Q1. How is General Communication different from Technical Communication?
Answer (from the study material):
General Communication: (1) Purpose is to build informal relations. (2) Not always has a specific
audience – e.g. poems and songs. (3) Informal in style, relaxed in approach. (4) Mostly oral. (5) Does
not have to be correct and concrete. (6) People forgive you in case of errors.
Technical Communication: (1) Always has a specific purpose related to business. (2) Always targets a
specific audience. (3) Always bound by format and protocol. (4) Both oral and written. (5) Must be
correct and concrete with facts, figures and graphs. (6) People think negatively if errors are made.
Simple Explanation (for your understanding):
General communication is what we use with friends and family – relaxed, and small mistakes are
usually forgiven. Technical communication is used at work or in academics, so it must always be
accurate, targeted to the right audience, and free of errors, because mistakes here are judged much
more strictly.
Q2. What is the role of Technical Communication, i.e. what are the benefits of good
professional communication?
Answer (from the study material):
The benefits of good professional communication are: task solved on time, promotion, good scores,
good customer relations, good relation with colleagues, conflict resolved, and new ideas to do a job.
Simple Explanation (for your understanding):
Simply put, if you communicate well at work or college, your tasks get done faster, you build better
relationships with people around you, problems get sorted out quickly, and you are more likely to be
noticed and rewarded for it.
Q3. Why do we need Technical Communication in everyday life – what is its purpose?
Answer (from the study material):
Technical communication is needed in everyday life because: we need to buy products or services from
others (e.g. talking to doctors, customer care service); we need to be in a profession for our livelihood,
where we communicate with our colleagues (e.g. discussion among a team of engineers at office); and
we need to get training to join a profession (e.g. studying in a college, where we also require technical
communication).
Simple Explanation (for your understanding):
Whether you are asking a doctor about your health, discussing a project with your teammates, or sitting
in a college classroom, you are already using technical communication – it is simply part of daily
professional and academic life, not something separate from it.

days.title: Flow of Communication – Vertical (Downward & Upward)
days.summary: Daily speech topic for Day 3 on Technical Communication fundamentals.
days.content:
English Initiative - Phase 3 | Week 1 | Page 4
 DAY 3
Flow of Communication – Vertical (Downward & Upward)
Source: Flow of Communication
Q1. What is meant by the “Flow of Communication” in an organization?
Answer (from the study material):
In an organization, information flows through different hierarchies, and it is also bound by protocol.
When we try to trace the direction of that flow, we call it the flow of organizational communication. There
are three types of flow: Vertical, Horizontal, and Diagonal.
Simple Explanation (for your understanding):
In any organization, information doesn’t travel randomly – it moves through a set structure of seniors
and juniors, following certain rules. When we track which direction a message travels in (up, down, or
sideways), that direction is called its “flow”.
Q2. What is Vertical Communication, and why is it important?
Answer (from the study material):
Vertical Communication is communication between immediate hierarchies, e.g. teacher and students, or
HOD and teachers. It is the strictest in terms of protocol, and forms a major part of the official
communication in any organization.
Simple Explanation (for your understanding):
This is communication that happens directly between one level and the very next level above or below it
– for example, your class teacher and you, not the Director and you directly. Because it is official, it must
follow proper protocol.
Q3. What is Downward Communication? Give an example and the formats used.
Answer (from the study material):
When the higher management issues orders, appointment letters, job-descriptions, notices, etc. to the
employees or students, we have downward communication. Example: the HOD instructs the teachers to
take assignments within the 4th to 6th of February; accordingly, teachers inform students the date and
syllabus. Formats used: letters, telephone calls, face-to-face interactions, online portal, bulletin boards,
notice, memo, etc.
Simple Explanation (for your understanding):
Downward communication simply flows from someone senior to someone junior – instructions, orders
or notices moving down the chain of command, the way an HOD’s instruction eventually reaches the
students through the teachers.
Q4. What is Upward Communication? Give an example, the formats used, and its
importance.
Answer (from the study material):
Upward communication happens when a subordinate communicates with the higher authorities above
him/her, e.g. submission of a report, placing a request for leaves, placing a requisition for departmental
necessities, or registering a grievance with higher management. Example: the student places a request
to the teacher for attendance-rectification. Formats used: letters, emails, reports; telephone calls are
avoided unless there is urgency. It is necessary for a functional link between higher authorities and

days.title: Flow of Communication – Horizontal, Diagonal, & Grapevine
days.summary: Daily speech topic for Day 4 on Technical Communication fundamentals.
days.content:
English Initiative - Phase 3 | Week 1 | Page 6
 DAY 4
Flow of Communication – Horizontal & Diagonal
Source: Flow of Communication
Q1. What is Horizontal (Peer) Communication? Give an example.
Answer (from the study material):
Horizontal Communication, or peer communication, happens between professional equals. Its target is
fast cooperation among peers. Example: two students discussing a project, or two faculties discussing
the routine.
Simple Explanation (for your understanding):
This is communication between people on the same level – not senior to junior, but equal to equal – like
two classmates working together on an assignment.
Q2. How strict is protocol in Horizontal Communication, and what formats are used?
Answer (from the study material):
Compared to vertical communication, horizontal communication is relaxed in protocol. Formats used:
face-to-face conversation, memos, telephone calls, and emails.
Simple Explanation (for your understanding):
Because it happens between equals, there is no need for the strict formality of a boss-subordinate
conversation – people can talk more freely and casually while still staying professional.
Q3. What are the pros and cons of Horizontal Communication?
Answer (from the study material):
Pros: fast transmission of information; works great in handling difficult situations; creates team-spirit
across departments. Cons: clash of egos – a slight misunderstanding may result in an ego-clash;
time-waste in gossiping.
Simple Explanation (for your understanding):
Working with equals is quick and builds teamwork, but because there is no clear senior-junior structure,
small disagreements can turn into ego clashes, and casual conversations can drift into time-wasting
gossip.
Q4. What is Diagonal Communication? Give examples of when it is used.
Answer (from the study material):
Diagonal Communication is communication taking place between non-immediate hierarchies.
Examples: a student and the Director; a faculty member and the Chairman. It is used in times of
urgency, and also during organizational events, when higher management interacts with employees to
cultivate goodwill. Formats used: face-to-face interaction, telephone.
Simple Explanation (for your understanding):
This is communication that skips levels – for instance, a student speaking directly to the Director instead
of going through the HOD first. It usually happens only when something is urgent or during special
events meant to build goodwill.

days.title: Barriers to Communication – Inter-personal & Intra-personal
days.summary: Daily speech topic for Day 5 on Technical Communication fundamentals.
days.content:
English Initiative - Phase 3 | Week 1 | Page 8
 DAY 5
Barriers to Communication – General Barriers
Source: Barriers to Communication (Interpersonal & Intrapersonal)
Q1. What is a “Barrier” or “Noise” in communication?
Answer (from the study material):
Whenever an interruption happens during communication, it is called a Barrier, or Noise. When a barrier
happens, we have partial or total failure of communication. There are two broad types of barriers:
General Barriers and Organizational Barriers.
Simple Explanation (for your understanding):
A barrier is anything that gets in the way of a message being understood correctly – it can stop the
message completely or just make part of it get lost or misunderstood.
Q2. What are the two types of General Barriers?
Answer (from the study material):
General Barriers are of two types: Inter-personal, which happens between 2 people, and
Intra-personal, which happens in one’s own mind.
Simple Explanation (for your understanding):
Interpersonal barriers need at least two people to occur – something goes wrong between the sender
and receiver. Intrapersonal barriers happen entirely inside one person’s own thinking, even before or
after the message is exchanged.
Q3. What are the five Interpersonal Barriers? Explain each with an example.
Answer (from the study material):
(1) Language Barrier – when we speak in a language that is not known, or less-known, to the receiver.
Eg.: a foreigner speaks in English to an illiterate villager; a teacher uses heavy, technical jargon
unknown to the students. (2) Channel Barrier – whenever there is a disturbance in the channel
connecting the sender and receiver. Eg.: mobile-network failure, postal department delays. (3) Cultural
Gap – misunderstanding between two people of different cultures due to lack of mutual knowledge of
their culture. Eg.: an American friend walks into an Indian home with her shoes on, without knowing it is
considered rude in India. (4) Physical Barrier – any natural situation that makes you physically
uncomfortable (too hot, cold, moist, or noisy), or being physically unwell, which makes you a bad sender
or receiver of the message. Eg.: you cannot hear your phone in traffic; you cannot complete your work
because of fever. (5) Emotional/Psychological Barrier – when you are in an extreme state of mind
(too happy, sad, angry or afraid), you become a bad sender or receiver of the message. Eg.: you were
too excited about the college fest that you forgot to take the class notes from your friend.
Simple Explanation (for your understanding):
All five of these need two people to be involved, and each one blocks the message in a different way –
through words not understood, a broken connection, a cultural misunderstanding, physical discomfort,
or a strong emotion clouding attention. To fix the language barrier specifically: adjust your language to
the receiver, explain technical terms to a new learner, and use enough non-verbal cues along with your
spoken words.
Q4. What are the three Intra-personal Barriers? Explain each with an example.

days.title: Organizational Barriers & Formal Networks of Communication
days.summary: Daily speech topic for Day 6 on Technical Communication fundamentals.
days.content:
English Initiative - Phase 3 | Week 1 | Page 10
 DAY 6
Organizational Barriers & Formal Networks of
Communication
Source: Barriers to Communication (Organizational); Formal Networks of Communication
Q1. What are the five Organizational Barriers? Explain each with an example.
Answer (from the study material):
(1) Too many transfer stations – when too many people come in between the original sender and the
receiver. Eg.: a teacher tells Student A to inform the class about a test date change, and the message
gets distorted by the time it reaches the class. Steps: talk to your target receiver directly, or use a written
message if you must pass it through someone. (2) Fear of superiors – when a new member fears
seniors/the boss and does not clear doubts, which harms performance. Eg.: a student does not clear his
doubts regarding studies out of fear, and scores low in exams. Steps: orientation programmes, seniors
taking responsibility to help juniors approach them freely, and encouraging discussion. (3) Negative
tendency / Group-ism – when people of one group behave negatively towards another group,
information may not pass through them. Eg.: not passing important information to members of a ‘rival’
club. Steps: organize more inter-departmental programmes. (4) Data overload – the human mind has a
fixed capacity to process information at a given time; once that limit crosses, attention begins to fail. Eg.:
a teacher trying to finish a large portion of the syllabus in one class, with students getting distracted
towards the end. (5) Improper medium used – e.g. calling your boss instead of emailing, unless it is an
emergency; or teaching an economics class through lecture and board-work instead of PPT with graphs
and charts. Overall step: always keep your target audience and your purpose of communication in mind.
Simple Explanation (for your understanding):
These barriers are common specifically inside offices and organizations: messages get distorted when
passed through too many people, juniors stay silent out of fear, groups refuse to share information with
rival groups, too much information overwhelms the listener, and using the wrong medium (like calling
instead of emailing) causes misunderstanding. Most of these are solved by communicating directly,
encouraging open discussion, and choosing the right amount and the right medium of information.
Q2. What are Formal Networks of Communication, and why is the information in them
considered reliable?
Answer (from the study material):
When we trace the route of formal communication in an organization, we get Formal Networks of
communication. The information is always authentic and accurate, and we can track the source of
information as well as its receiver. There are five types: Chain Network, Y Network, Wheel Network,
Circle Network, and All-Channel Network.
Simple Explanation (for your understanding):
Formal networks are the “official paths” a message follows inside an organization. Because these paths
are fixed and official, you can always trace exactly where a message started and who it reached, which
is why the information passing through them is trusted.

days.title: 7 Cs of Communication & Non-Verbal Communication
days.summary: Daily speech topic for Day 7 on Technical Communication fundamentals.
days.content:
English Initiative - Phase 3 | Week 1 | Page 12
 DAY 7
7 C’s of Communication & Non-Verbal Communication
Source: 7 C’s of Formal Communication; Non-Verbal Communication (Kinesics, Proxemics, Haptics,
Chronemics)
Q1. Why does Formal Communication need the “7 C’s”, and what are they?
Answer (from the study material):
Formal communication requires building rapport with the target audience. Rapport-building is necessary
to convince our clients that we are no-nonsense people in our jobs, and that they can trust us to get
their jobs done. The 7 C’s of Business Communication are: Conciseness, Clarity, Concreteness,
Correctness, Completeness, Consideration, and Courtesy.
Simple Explanation (for your understanding):
These 7 C’s are simply a checklist – if your message follows all of them, the person receiving it will trust
you, understand you clearly, and take you seriously as a professional.
Q2. What is Conciseness, and how can we achieve it?
Answer (from the study material):
Conciseness means “to-the-point” – we have to say things in as short a way as possible. Steps to
achieve conciseness: use key words; state important information first; delete over-polite phrases; delete
repetitions (using umbrella terms, pronouns, or abbreviations); cross out redundancies; and cut out
lengthy phrases. Eg.: instead of “My account balance got deducted because of activation of Hello tunes.
I did not request for the activation” (18 words), we write: “Unauthorized activation of Hello Tunes caused
balance-deduction in my account” (11 words).
Simple Explanation (for your understanding):
Being concise doesn’t mean leaving out information – it means saying the same thing using fewer,
sharper words, so the reader or listener gets the point quickly without wading through unnecessary
phrases.
Q3. What is Clarity, and how can we achieve it?
Answer (from the study material):
Clarity means a clear-cut message – no doubt in the reader of what you want to say, no double
meaning, no scope for confusion. Steps to achieve clarity: use a glossary for technical terms; focus on
answering the WH-questions (what, whom, when, where, how, how many); use examples from daily life;
and use pictures and info-graphics such as graphs, pie-charts, bullets and flowcharts.
Simple Explanation (for your understanding):
A message has clarity when there is only one possible way to understand it. Explaining technical words,
answering the basic who/what/when/where questions, and adding visuals all help remove any confusion
from your message.

OFFICIAL STUDY MATERIAL (as given in your lecture slides / sample files)
‘Resume’ means “Short Summary”
 • Used by technical professionals.
• Contains organized information about one’s qualification, experience and skills.
• Order of the above is adjusted according to the needs of the applicant.
• Ranges from one to two pages.
3 Types of Resume
 • Reverse Chronological
• Functional
• Combination-style
1. Reverse-Chronological Resume
 • Most commonly used.
• Educational details, projects and experiences are mentioned first, in reverse chronology.
• Skills are mentioned later.
• Used by freshers; people with a clear and single career-outline, with no breaks.
 Sample of a Reverse-Chronological Resume (given in your lecture slides)
2. Functional Resume
 • Mentions skills and work-experience first.

---
MYTH English Initiative | Phase 3 | Unit 2 and 3 | Page 8
Which type should you use? You are B.Tech students and freshers, so the Reverse-Chronological
format is the best choice for you: Education, then Projects, then Experience (if any), then Skills.

 • Define a resume. (Short summary of qualification, experience and skills, 1 to 2 pages.)
• Name the three types of resume and differentiate them in a table.

professionals?

days.title: Resume Writing Guidelines & ATS Friendly Formatting
days.content:
MYTH English Initiative | Phase 3 | Unit 2 and 3 | Page 9
DAY 9 | TUESDAY
WEEK 2
ATS-Friendly Resume and Strategic Resume Upgrading
Source: Resume & Cover Letter lecture (slides 11 to 14)
1. READ
about 15 minutes
2. RECORD
about 15 minutes (speak 2 to 10 min)
3. SEND + SELF-ANALYSIS
mandatory
OFFICIAL STUDY MATERIAL (as given in your lecture slides / sample files)
ATS Friendly Resume
An Applicant Tracking System (ATS) is software that companies use to collect, organize, and initially
screen large numbers of job applications.
Consider a B.Tech CSE student applying for a Software Development Intern position. Suppose the job
description asks for Python, SQL, Git, REST APIs, problem-solving, and teamwork.
First Step: Identify which of these requirements you genuinely possess, which you can prove in your
resume. This strategy is called relevance and keyword alignment.
2nd Step: Data organization. Use standard headings such as Education, Technical Skills, Projects,
Internships, and Certifications, helping the ATS locate information accurately. Order of these headings will
depend on whether you are going for a chronological / functional / combinational resume.
3rd Step: Evidence with action verbs. Use words like Developed, Designed, Tested, Implemented, and
Analyzed to enlist your provable skills and knowledge.
4th Step: Formatting. Use a simple layout, clear spacings, bold-facing on headings only, and brief
descriptions. This positively impacts the recruiter impression.
Strategic Resume Upgrading: From “Having a Resume” to “Building Evidence”
A strong resume is a record of career growth. B.Tech CSE students should first identify a target master skill
area (for example, AI/ML, cybersecurity, software development, cloud computing, data analytics, or product
engineering) and then strategically build evidence around it.
Steps to Evolve Resume Strategically
i. Set a clear skill goal: Choose a specific target such as “AI/ML internship by the end of third year” and
map the required skills: Python, Statistics, Machine Learning, SQL, TensorFlow/PyTorch, and relevant
projects.
ii. Build proof-worthy skills: Do not merely list “Python – Good knowledge.” Show where you applied it:
Skill → Application → Evidence → Outcome.
iii. Build projects around the goal: Select academic, personal, hackathon, or internship projects that
demonstrate your target skill area rather than collecting unrelated activities.
iv. Quantify your impact: Wherever possible, show users reached, percentage improvement, time saved,
accuracy achieved, datasets processed, team size, events conducted, people trained, rankings, or project
duration.
v. Create a coherent career story: Your resume should show a progression from Goal → Skills →
Projects/Experience → Evidence → Impact, rather than appearing as a random collection of courses,
certificates, and activities.

---
MYTH English Initiative | Phase 3 | Unit 2 and 3 | Page 11
• v. Create a coherent career story. Your resume should read like a story with a clear line: Goal →
Skills → Projects/Experience → Evidence → Impact, not like a random bag of certificates.
EXAM TIP: Exam answer for “ATS-friendly resume”: write the definition of ATS, then the four steps in
order (relevance and keyword alignment; data organization; evidence with action verbs; formatting), and
add one example. For “strategic upgrading”: write the five steps (goal, proof-worthy skills, goal-based
projects, quantified impact, coherent story).
VIDEO TASK: DAY 9
Speak for 2 to 10 minutes in your own words (do not read aloud). Cover these points:
 1. What is an ATS and why do companies use it?
2. Explain the four steps of an ATS-friendly resume with one example of a job description.
3. Take one skill you have and explain it as Skill → Application → Evidence → Outcome.
4. Which target skill area will you choose, and what evidence will you build for it in the next six months?
After recording: send the video in the group with “Day 9” in your message, then do your self-analysis
(mandatory).

days.title: Cover Letter Writing & Structure
days.content:
MYTH English Initiative | Phase 3 | Unit 2 and 3 | Page 16
DAY 11 | THURSDAY
WEEK 2
Cover Letter
Source: Resume & Cover Letter lecture (slides 15 to 21) and the sample cover letter given by your teacher
1. READ
about 15 minutes
2. RECORD
about 15 minutes (speak 2 to 10 min)
3. SEND + SELF-ANALYSIS
mandatory
OFFICIAL STUDY MATERIAL (as given in your lecture slides / sample files)
Definition
 • A cover letter is a formal letter from the applicant to the company, expressing interest for the job.
• It is of two types: Solicited and Unsolicited.
Cover Letter: Solicited vs. Unsolicited
 • Solicited: Written in response to an advertisement.
• Unsolicited: Written in tentative anticipation of a vacancy.
Cover Letter: 1st Paragraph
 • If Solicited: mention the date and name of the paper/webpage where you saw the advertisement. Then
express your interest for the position in the next line.
• If Unsolicited: mention what inspired you to apply in the company, and what training you have to get
selected for the post.
Middle Paragraph
Write in details the following:
 • Educational Qualification
• Projects and internships done as a student
• Some strengths, i.e. team spirit, communication skills, etc.
Closing of Cover Letter
 • Insist on an interview call to discuss work options.
• Sign off.
• In the end, mention ‘Enclosed: Resume’.

---
MYTH English Initiative | Phase 3 | Unit 2 and 3 | Page 19
Closing paragraph. Politely request an interview call to discuss work options. The slide uses the word
‘insist’, but in a formal letter it means to request strongly and politely, not to demand. Then sign off, and
at the end write ‘Enclosed: Resume’, which tells the reader that a resume is attached.
4. Reading the sample cover letters
Teacher’s sample (internship at an event company). It has these parts in order: Your Address, Date,
Recipient’s Address, salutation (‘Respected Sir,’), Subject line, three short paragraphs, a closing line,
‘Regards,’, the name, course and college, and finally the enclosure line (‘encl: Resume’).
 • Paragraph 1: the wish to apply as an intern, the present course and the skills (communication and
organizational skills).
• Paragraph 2: proof, that is projects related to events and active part in organizing events at the college
level.
• Paragraph 3: the resume is attached and the writer waits for a reply.
Second sample (lecture slide). This letter is addressed to a named person (‘Dear Mr. Franklin’) and refers
to a position posted by the university’s Career Services Center, so it is a solicited letter. It describes the
degree and relevant courses, the hands-on work the student does in the university’s prototyping facility,
and why the internship would help; finally it mentions the attached resume, asks for an interview and gives
contact details.
EXAM TIP: Parts of a formal letter, to remember: sender’s address, date, receiver’s address, salutation,
subject line, body, closing, signature, enclosure. In your own letter, write your own name and enclose
your own resume.
5. Do and don’t
 • Do keep it short (one page), polite and specific to the company.
• Do not repeat the resume line by line; add the ‘why’ behind it.
• Do not make spelling or grammar mistakes; a careless letter suggests a careless worker.
• If possible, address a named person instead of a general title.
VIDEO TASK: DAY 11
Speak for 2 to 10 minutes in your own words (do not read aloud). Cover these points:
 1. What is a cover letter, and how is it different from a resume?
2. Explain solicited and unsolicited cover letters with one example each.
3. Tell what you will write in the first, middle and closing paragraph for an internship you want.
4. Why do we write ‘Enclosed: Resume’ at the end?
After recording: send the video in the group with “Day 11” in your message, then do your self-analysis
(mandatory).

Effective Profiling (LinkedIn Presence)
Source: Effective Profiling and Network Building lecture (slides 2 to 4)
1. READ
about 15 minutes
2. RECORD
about 15 minutes (speak 2 to 10 min)
3. SEND + SELF-ANALYSIS
mandatory
OFFICIAL STUDY MATERIAL (as given in your lecture slides / sample files)
Definition
Designing your public profile over professional social media platforms like LinkedIn. Steps include:
 • Header section: Mentioning skill and experience related keywords in the header, to make the profile
Search Engine Optimized.
• Main Body: Strategic write-up of the ‘About you’ section, which keeps a perfect balance of passion and
concrete skill-sets.
• Active posts: (i) Announcing achievements; (ii) Getting endorsements; (iii) Maintaining blog-posts on
areas of interest [This shows your interest in trending market features. Hence, it shows your
adaptability.]
Benefits of Profiling
 • Clarity of career goals / research interests.
• Better networking with similar people of domain knowledge or interest. Helps in getting projects.
• Competitive edge: SEO keywords enable better visibility of profile in job and internship calls.
• Branding: You are not just another job-hunter with a list of academic and project details. You are a
go-getter with achieved success, endorsed skills and specific goals.
General pointers to know for Profiling
i. SWOT Analysis: to highlight strengths and market-ready skills on the header, and to do necessary work
(certifications, internships etc.) to bypass your weakness and market-threats.
ii. Short-term and Long-term goals: use your SWOT analysis to predict what challenges you can face to
stay viable in the market. Use your strong points to gather experience-hours and certifications. Selecting
projects and certifications are your short-term goals. Long-term goal is to stay competitive.
iii. Networking: Following industry big-shots; actively blogging on trending topics or research interests.
People-power makes you visible in the era of virtual job market.
iv. Mentorship: Getting a mentor to review your profile / career path helps.
TEACHER’S EXPLANATION (to understand the topic deeply)
1. What is ‘profiling’?
Your resume is a paper document that you send to one company. Your LinkedIn profile is a public,
online resume that every recruiter, teacher and professional can search and see at any time. ‘Profiling’
means designing this public profile with care, so that people get the right picture of you in a few seconds.

---
MYTH English Initiative | Phase 3 | Unit 2 and 3 | Page 22

 1. What is profiling, and why is a LinkedIn profile like an online resume?
2. Explain the three parts of a good profile: header, About section, and active posts.
3. Do a SWOT analysis of yourself in simple words.
4. Write and say aloud the header line you would use on your own profile.

days.title: Professional Networking & Relationship Building
days.content:
MYTH English Initiative | Phase 3 | Unit 2 and 3 | Page 23
DAY 13 | SATURDAY
WEEK 2
Professional Networking (Part 1): Why It Matters and How
to Do It
Source: ‘Communication and Networking: Building Relationships in Career Development’ by Dr. Smita Mishra;
Effective Profiling and Network Building lecture
1. READ
about 15 minutes
2. RECORD
about 15 minutes (speak 2 to 10 min)
3. SEND + SELF-ANALYSIS
mandatory
OFFICIAL STUDY MATERIAL (as given in your lecture slides / sample files)
Communication and Networking
 • It involves maintaining your connections of batchmates and colleagues over professional and social
media platforms.
• Also includes making new connections during various social events, conferences, competitions, etc.
Effective communication and networking are essential for career development. This presentation explores:
(1) strategies for building professional relationships; (2) maintaining professional relationships and
overcoming barriers; (3) developing a personal brand.
Why Communication and Networking Matter?
 • 1. Growth Opportunities: Networking exposes you to new ideas, opportunities, and potential mentors
or collaborators.
• 2. Job Prospects: Strong communication skills and a robust professional network can open doors to
new career opportunities.
• 3. Personal Branding: An effective network and good communication skills help you establish a strong
personal brand.
• 4. Knowledge Sharing: Communication with peers and mentors facilitates the exchange of knowledge,
insights, and best practices.
Strategies for Effective Communication and Networking
 • Identify Objectives: Define clear career objectives and determine the type of connections needed to
achieve them.
• Asking Meaningful Questions: Ask thoughtful questions to show genuine interest and foster engaging
conversations.
• Non-Verbal Communication: Pay attention to your body language, gestures, and eye contact to
convey confidence and sincerity.
• Active Listening: Engage in active listening to understand others better and build stronger
connections.
• Build a Network: Attend industry events, seminars, and workshops to meet like-minded individuals and
experts.
• Nurture Relationships: Maintain regular communication with contacts, showing genuine interest in
their work and progress.
Benefits of Building Relationships and Networking
 • Career Growth: Networking opens doors to career advancement opportunities, including promotions
and leadership roles. Example: A project manager secures a leadership position through
recommendations from professional contacts.

---
MYTH English Initiative | Phase 3 | Unit 2 and 3 | Page 25
EXAM TIP: In the exam, write the four reasons (growth, jobs, branding, knowledge sharing) in one
paragraph, then list the six strategies, and give at least two of the examples above. Teachers like points
that are backed with an example.
EXTRA (not in the slides): A small action plan for a student: this week, (1) update your LinkedIn header;
(2) message two seniors or alumni with one genuine question each; (3) attend one online or offline event;
(4) write down what you learned and send a thank-you note.
VIDEO TASK: DAY 13
Speak for 2 to 10 minutes in your own words (do not read aloud). Cover these points:
 1. What is professional networking? Explain the difference between a contact and a relationship.
2. Explain the four reasons why communication and networking matter.
3. Choose any three of the six strategies and explain each with an example.
4. Tell one real or imaginary situation where networking can help a B.Tech student.

(mandatory).

days.title: Overcoming Communication Barriers in Professional Networking
days.content:
MYTH English Initiative | Phase 3 | Unit 2 and 3 | Page 26
DAY 14 | MONDAY
WEEK 3
Professional Networking (Part 2): Personal Brand,
Relationships, New Connections and Barriers
Source: Dr. Smita Mishra’s presentation; Effective Profiling and Network Building lecture
1. READ
about 15 minutes
2. RECORD
about 15 minutes (speak 2 to 10 min)
3. SEND + SELF-ANALYSIS
mandatory
OFFICIAL STUDY MATERIAL (as given in your lecture slides / sample files)
Developing Your Personal Brand
 • Showcase Your Unique Skills: Highlight your talents and expertise to make an impression in your
industry.
• Create a Strong Online Presence: Build a professional website and optimize your social media profiles
to represent your brand effectively.
• Consistency is Key: Use consistent messaging, visuals, and tone to establish a recognisable and
reliable personal brand.
Building and Maintaining Professional Relationships
 • 1. Initiate Contact: Reach out and introduce yourself to industry professionals you admire or
colleagues with shared interests.
• 2. Nurture Connections: Stay in touch by attending industry events, sending personalized messages,
and offering support.
• 3. Provide Value: Offer assistance, share resources, and connect individuals within your network to
foster a sense of reciprocity.
Strategies to Build New Connections
 Strategies to build new connections (lecture slide)
• Planning part: (a) Identify common talking points, like research interests, domain knowledge. (b) Think
of relevant questions to ask. It should relate to your long-term career goals and short-term steps.
• Action part: (a) Non-verbal cues should indicate interest. You are talking to learn, not to click pictures.
(b) Active listening: includes note-taking; exchanging emails; fast processing of the information spoken,
to ask deeper questions.

---
MYTH English Initiative | Phase 3 | Unit 2 and 3 | Page 28
• Action part (during the meeting): show interest through non-verbal cues. The line ‘you are talking to
learn, not to click pictures’ means: the purpose of meeting is learning, not collecting photos. Listen
actively: take notes, exchange email addresses, and think quickly about what you heard, so that you can
ask a deeper question.
4. Barriers to networking and how to remove them
Both presentations list similar barriers. Learn them together:
Barrier
Solution given in the slides
Fear of rejection
Networking involves risk; treat rejection as a learning opportunity. Connect over
platforms or events where you can show your skills, so that your request is more
likely to be accepted.
Lack of confidence / sense of
self-worth
Have faith in your skills, keep upgrading them, practise self-affirmation, and take
feedback and support from a mentor or trusted friend. Be generous in self-praise
and specific in self-criticism.
Time constraints
Use small pockets of time; start with small events or those that relate to your
short-term goals.
Shyness / introverted nature
Begin with virtual platforms and blogs, then calls, then in-person meetings. Start
with small events or one-to-one connections. Be responsive when needed and
resourceful when delivering commitments.
‘Generous in self-praise, specific in self-criticism’ means: do not be shy to accept your strengths, but
when you criticize yourself, name the exact point (for example, ‘I speak too fast during introductions’)
instead of saying ‘I am bad at communication’. A specific point can be fixed.
EXAM TIP: A good exam answer on barriers: name the four barriers, give one solution for each from the
table, and end with one sentence on why networking is worth the effort.
VIDEO TASK: DAY 14
Speak for 2 to 10 minutes in your own words (do not read aloud). Cover these points:
 1. Explain what a personal brand is and the three tools to build it.
2. Explain the three steps of building and maintaining professional relationships. What does ‘reciprocity’
mean?
3. You are going to meet a professional at an event. Explain your planning part and your action part.
4. Which networking barrier do you face most, and how will you overcome it?
After recording: send the video in the group with “Day 14” in your message, then do your self-analysis
(mandatory).

days.title: Critical Soft Skills for Engineers
days.content:
MYTH English Initiative | Phase 3 | Unit 2 and 3 | Page 29
DAY 15 | TUESDAY
WEEK 3
Interview Skills (Part 1): Questions That Test Behaviour,
Categories 1 to 4
Source: Interview Round lecture (overview slide and slides 3 to 6)
1. READ
about 15 minutes
2. RECORD
about 15 minutes (speak 2 to 10 min)
3. SEND + SELF-ANALYSIS
mandatory
OFFICIAL STUDY MATERIAL (as given in your lecture slides / sample files)
Questions Testing Behaviour Patterns. The lecture divides interview questions into nine categories. The
percentages in the picture show the share of each category.
 Questions Testing Behaviour Patterns (lecture slide)
1. Self-awareness & Professional Identity
A clear professional identity helps candidates present their experience confidently and realistically, while
demonstrating maturity, reflection, and readiness for continued professional growth.
Frequent questions: Introduce yourself. / What are your greatest strengths? / What is one area you are
improving? / What achievement are you most proud of? / What work environment brings out your best? /
What would your colleagues say about you?
2. Career Motivation & Organizational Alignment
HR wants to know why you want the organization, whether your expectations are realistic, and whether you
are likely to remain committed.
Frequent questions: Why do you want to work with us? / Why should we hire you? / Where do you see
yourself five years from now? / What would you do after receiving a better offer six months later? / How
would you handle a family emergency after relocation? / What are you looking for in your next role?

---
MYTH English Initiative | Phase 3 | Unit 2 and 3 | Page 31
4. Category 3: Adaptability & Learning Agility
What the interviewer checks: Can you learn fast and stay productive when things change? Technology
changes quickly, so this matters a lot.
How to answer: Give a real example of something you learned recently (a language, a tool, a framework)
and how you learned it. The question ‘How did your resume upgrade in the last 12 months?’ connects to
Day 9: show new projects, certificates or skills added in a year. For change in role, say you would first
understand the change, ask questions and adjust.
5. Category 4: Problem-solving & Decision-making
What the interviewer checks: The slide says that when AI handles routine tasks, human judgment
becomes more valuable. So interviewers want to see how you think when a problem is difficult, new or
unclear.
How to answer: Explain your thinking in steps: understand the problem, list the options, compare them
(cost, time, risk), choose one and give the reason. For ‘Why did you select this project topic?’ give a clear
reason and the problem it solves. For ‘the next best alternative to your tech-stack’, name another tool or
language and compare it honestly with your choice; this shows that you did not choose blindly.
EXAM TIP: In the exam, write the category name, one line on what the interviewer wants to know, and
two example questions. In a real interview, prepare one real story for each of these four categories.
VIDEO TASK: DAY 15
Speak for 2 to 10 minutes in your own words (do not read aloud). Cover these points:
 1. Explain why interviewers ask questions that test behaviour. Which categories are tested the most,
according to the picture?
2. Answer aloud: ‘Introduce yourself.’
3. Answer aloud: ‘What is one area you are improving?’
4. Answer aloud: ‘Why did you select your project topic?’ or ‘What skill have you recently learned?’
After recording: send the video in the group with “Day 15” in your message, then do your self-analysis
(mandatory).

days.title: Adaptability & Continuous Learning
days.content:
MYTH English Initiative | Phase 3 | Unit 2 and 3 | Page 32
DAY 16 | WEDNESDAY
WEEK 3
Interview Skills (Part 2): Questions That Test Behaviour,
Categories 5 to 9
Source: Interview Round lecture (slides 7 to 11)
1. READ
about 15 minutes
2. RECORD
about 15 minutes (speak 2 to 10 min)
3. SEND + SELF-ANALYSIS
mandatory
OFFICIAL STUDY MATERIAL (as given in your lecture slides / sample files)
5. Communication Competence
This header tests whether candidates can listen, explain ideas clearly, adjust language, handle
misunderstandings, and communicate professionally.
Frequent questions: How would you handle disagreement with a colleague or client? / What would you do if
your message were misunderstood? / Introduce yourself. / Tell me about a time you explained something
complicated.
6. Emotional Intelligence
Organizations depend on collaboration, empathy, active listening, and emotional control. Interviewers
therefore examine how candidates handle disagreements, criticism, difficult people, and team
responsibilities.
Frequent questions: Have you ever settled a disagreement within the team? / If I ask about you, what will I
learn from your professor? From your team mates? / How do you handle criticism? / How would you handle
an angry customer?
7. Reliability
Candidates should demonstrate responsibility through real examples rather than simply claiming they are
hardworking.
Frequently asked questions: What would you do if a deadline became impossible? / How do you maintain
quality under pressure? / Tell me about a mistake you made. What did you learn?
8. Initiative and Leadership
Organizations value employees who identify problems, suggest improvements, take responsible action,
and influence others positively.
Frequent questions: Tell me about taking initiative without being asked. / Describe making an important
decision quickly. / Did you ever provide back-up to your team?
9. Integrity and Professionalism
Interviewers may present uncomfortable situations to understand how candidates behave when rules,
personal preferences, workplace pressures, or ethical responsibilities come into conflict.
Frequent questions: What would you do if a colleague violated a rule? / How would you protect confidential
information? / Would you lie for the company? / Would you report your company, if you suspect
wrongdoing?
Note: In the original slides, this last category is numbered ‘7’ by mistake. In the ‘Questions Testing
Behaviour Patterns’ picture (Day 15), it is category number 9.

---

 1. Explain any three of the categories 5 to 9 and tell what the interviewer wants to check in each.
2. Answer aloud: ‘Tell me about a mistake you made. What did you learn?’
3. Answer aloud: ‘How do you handle criticism?’
4. Answer aloud: ‘Tell me about taking initiative without being asked.’

days.title: Technical Reports - Definition, Types & Structure
days.content:
MYTH English Initiative | Phase 3 | Unit 2 and 3 | Page 35
DAY 17 | THURSDAY
WEEK 3
Group Discussion: Meaning, Types and Selection-Process
GD
Source: Group Discussion lecture (slides 2 to 10)
1. READ
about 15 minutes
2. RECORD
about 15 minutes (speak 2 to 10 min)
3. SEND + SELF-ANALYSIS
mandatory
OFFICIAL STUDY MATERIAL (as given in your lecture slides / sample files)
GD: Definition
A group interaction of more than two people, that involves decision making and problem solving in a
collective manner. It uses: Team working skills; Initiative taking; Communication skills; Critical thinking
skills.
Major GD Types: TWO
 • Selection Process GD
• Project-based Team Discussion
Selection process: what is tested?
 • Communication skills
• Team work
• Initiative taking
• Creative thinking
• Ability to talk logically, with valid points
• Listening skills
• Attitude adjustment
Selection process GD: 4 Types
 • Factual
• Controversial
• Abstract
• Case based
Factual GD: Based on current affairs. Gives a candidate a chance to prove awareness of events around
him / her. E.g. The National Educational Policy.
Controversial GD: Argumentative in nature. Target: to check how a candidate handles the situation, when
someone does not agree with him/her on an issue. E.g. Reservations should be removed. Women make
better managers.
Abstract GD: Hypothetical topics. Open ended. Candidates come up with what the topic means to them,
and why. Tests creative thinking skills. E.g. Sky is green; the number 10.
Case-based GD: Tests managerial skills. A case is given, where there is a conflict situation in an office.
Candidates discuss on the best course of action. Target: to test the candidate’s (i) ability to visualize
long-term and short-term consequences of an action; (ii) ability to think from ethical and professional angles
while solving a problem.

---
MYTH English Initiative | Phase 3 | Unit 2 and 3 | Page 37
EXAM TIP: Exam tip: write the definition, the two major types, the seven tested qualities, and then the
four types with one example each.
VIDEO TASK: DAY 17
Speak for 2 to 10 minutes in your own words (do not read aloud). Cover these points:
 1. What is a group discussion, and what is the difference between the two major types?
2. List the seven qualities tested in a selection GD and explain any four.
3. Explain the four types of selection GD with one example topic for each.
4. Choose one controversial-type topic. Tell how you would disagree politely without becoming angry.
After recording: send the video in the group with “Day 17” in your message, then do your self-analysis
(mandatory).

days.title: Feasibility Reports & Technical Progress Reports
days.content:
MYTH English Initiative | Phase 3 | Unit 2 and 3 | Page 38
DAY 18 | FRIDAY
WEEK 3
Project-Based Team Discussion: The Five Stages
Source: Group Discussion lecture (slides 11 to 17)
1. READ
about 15 minutes
2. RECORD
about 15 minutes (speak 2 to 10 min)
3. SEND + SELF-ANALYSIS
mandatory
OFFICIAL STUDY MATERIAL (as given in your lecture slides / sample files)
5 Stages of Team-Discussion
i. Forming ii. Storming iii. Norming iv. Performing v. Adjourning
i. Forming
Members come together and try to understand the task, people and expectations.
E.g.: In a 4-member B.Tech team for a hackathon, each member comes with a unique skill: A knows
Python; B is skilled in UI/UX; C has knowledge of machine learning; D is good in research and
presentation. At this stage, they discuss: “What problem should we solve?” “Who will build what?”
 • Nobody wants to dominate the conversation yet. Roles are still unclear.
• Team state: high enthusiasm, low clarity.
ii. Storming
Differences emerge over ideas, roles, leadership, workload and priorities. Conflict is common. Questions
explored: ‘Whose idea should be followed?’
E.g.: A wants to build an AI healthcare prediction tool. B argues that a student-placement assistant app will
be a better idea, as a healthcare app will be too complicated. C thinks that some of the app-detailing of the
student app will overcomplicate the backend. D feels the team is not listening to her requirements of data
for the presentation.
iii. Norming
The group establishes working rules, roles, communication patterns and shared expectations.
E.g.: The B.Tech team agrees on the student-placement assistant app idea. They go ahead to create rules
for themselves: A will take care of the ML component; B will handle backend/API integration; C will work on
the interface; D will handle research and presentation. For every major technical decision, the team will
need an agreement.
iv. Performing
The team becomes functional and task-focused. Members trust one another and collaborate effectively.
This is the stage to test and troubleshoot any glitches within the time-frame of the hackathon. The members
work as a seamless support-system for each other, to deliver the project-pipeline for demonstration.
E.g.: C discovers that the ML model is performing poorly. Instead of blaming him, A quickly suggests that
the model be simplified and the API response be improved. The other members adjust accordingly.
v. Adjourning
The task ends. Members reflect, celebrate, document learning or move on.

---
MYTH English Initiative | Phase 3 | Unit 2 and 3 | Page 40
4. Why is the model useful? (the two benefits)
 • It tells you exactly where the group is stuck. Instead of saying ‘this team is terrible because we argue
a lot’, you can say ‘we are in the storming stage’. This is a normal stage, and the way out is norming:
clear rules and roles.
• It encourages collaboration instead of competition among team members.
EXAM TIP: Exam tip: list the five stages in order and write one or two lines with one example for each. A
table like the one above scores well because it is clear. Remember the order with the first letters F, S, N,
P, A.
VIDEO TASK: DAY 18
Speak for 2 to 10 minutes in your own words (do not read aloud). Cover these points:
 1. Why is project-based team discussion different from a selection GD?
2. Explain the five stages in order with the hackathon example.
3. In which stage do you think your own team (or class group) is right now, and why?
4. Explain the two benefits of this model.
After recording: send the video in the group with “Day 18” in your message, then do your self-analysis
(mandatory).

days.title: Memo Reports & Business Communication
days.content:
MYTH English Initiative | Phase 3 | Unit 2 and 3 | Page 41
DAY 19 | SATURDAY
WEEK 3
Report Writing: Purposes, Formats and the Memo Report
Source: Report Writing lecture; Memo format and Sample Memo Report given by your teacher
1. READ
about 15 minutes
2. RECORD
about 15 minutes (speak 2 to 10 min)
3. SEND + SELF-ANALYSIS
mandatory
OFFICIAL STUDY MATERIAL (as given in your lecture slides / sample files)
What is a report?
A document that reports an event that has already happened. The PURPOSES of writing a report are: 1.
Informational 2. Situational 3. Analytical Report.
Informational Purpose
They provide a brief summary of things, without offering any analysis. E.g.: progress report; employee
performance appraisal.
Situational Purposes
Reports written in an emergency, like accident, labor unrest, etc. They provide recommendation, not
analysis.
Analytical Report
They investigate the root cause for a trouble, and suggest solutions. E.g.: Troubleshooting reports;
Evaluative reports; Feasibility reports; Brand performance reports.
Formats of Report
Three formats: 1. Memo format [very short] 2. Letter format [medium] 3. Manuscript format [long].
Formats of a report depend on its recipient and scope.
1. Memo Report
 • Memos are especially important when you need to give information quickly or require a fast response.
• The recipient is a fellow member of the organization.

---

3. Explain the sections of a memo report using the sample about the food kiosk.

days.title: Technical Proposals - Definition, Purpose & Types
days.content:
MYTH English Initiative | Phase 3 | Unit 2 and 3 | Page 46
DAY 20 | MONDAY
WEEK 4
Technical Proposal Writing (Part 1): Meaning, Purposes,
Types and Structure
Source: Proposal Writing lecture (slides 2 to 11)
1. READ
about 15 minutes
2. RECORD
about 15 minutes (speak 2 to 10 min)
3. SEND + SELF-ANALYSIS
mandatory
OFFICIAL STUDY MATERIAL (as given in your lecture slides / sample files)
Definition
A proposal is a written document that gets: (a) permission to do a construction project; (b) grants to do a
research work; (c) permission to become a supplier. A proposal always offers to solve a problem.
The various Purposes of Proposal
 Purposes
Used for
To survey; To plan
Construction project on behalf of the Government
To improve
Research work; Business plans
To sell; To train
Become a supplier of services or materials to a company
3 Types of Proposals
 • Sales Proposals
• Research Proposals
• Business Proposals
A proposal can be Solicited or Un-Solicited.
Solicited Proposals
When we write a proposal in response to an advertisement, it is called a Solicited Proposal. Such ads,
called RFP [Request for Proposals], are floated by organizations, when they need material, services, or
research ideas.
Un-Solicited Proposal
When we place our proposal out of our own interest, without any ad, it is called an Un-Solicited Proposal.
Characteristics of a good Proposal
 • Shows need-fulfillment of the customer.
• Points out gains in terms of: Efficiency; Money; Prestige.
• Mentions details like cost, working methods, etc.
• Creative.
• Pro-active in tone, to connect with the customer.

---
MYTH English Initiative | Phase 3 | Unit 2 and 3 | Page 48
An easy way to remember: Prefatory = what the reader sees first (title, letter, contents, summary). Main
Body = the plan (what, how, who, how much, final word). Supplementary = proof and help at the end
(appendix, references, glossary).
EXAM TIP: Exam tip: if a question says ‘Explain the structure of a technical proposal’, draw the
three-column table first, and then explain each item in one line. You will do this tomorrow.
VIDEO TASK: DAY 20
Speak for 2 to 10 minutes in your own words (do not read aloud). Cover these points:
 1. What is a proposal? How is it different from a report?
2. Explain solicited and unsolicited proposals and RFP with examples.
3. List the characteristics of a good proposal.
4. Name the three parts of a proposal structure and the items in each part.
After recording: send the video in the group with “Day 20” in your message, then do your self-analysis
(mandatory).

days.title: Proposal Structure (Prefatory Parts, Body, Supplementary)
days.content:
MYTH English Initiative | Phase 3 | Unit 2 and 3 | Page 49
DAY 21 | TUESDAY
WEEK 4
Technical Proposal Writing (Part 2): Parts in Detail and the
Proposal Format
Source: Proposal Writing lecture (slides 12 to 21) and the Technical Proposal format given by your teacher
1. READ
about 15 minutes
2. RECORD
about 15 minutes (speak 2 to 10 min)
3. SEND + SELF-ANALYSIS
mandatory
OFFICIAL STUDY MATERIAL (as given in your lecture slides / sample files)
Prefatory Parts
Title page: Contains topic, name of the person writing the proposal; his/her company logo; the name of the
receiver; time of submission.
Letter of Transmittal: A cover letter to the receiver, mentioning the advertisement and the proposal
outline.
Table of Contents & List of Illustration: Marks page numbers for the verbal and picture-contents.
Executive Summary: An abstract for the proposal. A two-page outline of the proposal.
Main Body
1. Introduction
 • 1a. Problem & Need: Specifies the problem it targets to solve; and why the proposer’s solution is
unique.
• 1b. Background: Gives a history about the problem, and others’ efforts to solve it.
• 1c. Objectives: The technological, social and economic goals of the project.
• 1d. Scope and limitation: Outlines the technical boundaries of the project.
2. Technical Procedure
 • 2a. Methods & Sources: Mentions the technology, process, etc. you will use to complete the project.
• 2b. Plan: Sets timeline for each step.
3. Managerial Procedure
 • Mentions your requirements of: labor, equipment, infrastructure.
• Also mentions the qualifications of your team-members who are going to execute the project.
4. Cost Estimate
 • Gives a table of cost break-up, required by you.
• Sections covered by it are: raw materials, wage, transport, equipment, contingencies.
Conclusion: Summarizes your proposal to be a good deal for the customer.
Supplementary Parts
 • Appendix: Attachment of any extra data related to your project proposal.
• References: Citation of information sources.
• Glossary: Explains the technical terms in easy language.

---
MYTH English Initiative | Phase 3 | Unit 2 and 3 | Page 52
4. Reading your teacher’s proposal format
The format is a short, student-friendly version of the same structure:
 • First the title block (Proposal Title, Submitted by, Submitted to, Date of Submission), then a Table of
Contents with section names and page numbers.
• Executive Summary.
• 1. Introduction: Problem & Need, Objectives, Scope, Limitations.
• 2. Technical Procedure: Methods & Process, and a Plan & Timeline table with the columns Phase,
Activity and Duration (the sample rows are: 1st Week, 1 week; 2nd–3rd Week, 2 weeks; 4th Week, 1
week).
• 3. Managerial Procedure: In-Charge, Supporting Members, Infrastructure Required.
• 4. Cost Estimate: a table with Item, Quantity and Estimated Cost, ending with a total.
• 5. Conclusion, then Appendix, References and Glossary.
EXAM TIP: The lecture slides list Background inside the Introduction, but the short format does not have
a separate Background line. This is only because the format is a short version. In the exam, write the full
list of the slides, and in a practical task, follow the format given by your teacher.
Practice idea: choose a small idea (for example, a one-month coding workshop for juniors). Fill the format
in your notebook: problem, objective, plan for four weeks, who is in charge, what infrastructure you need,
and a small cost table.
VIDEO TASK: DAY 21
Speak for 2 to 10 minutes in your own words (do not read aloud). Cover these points:
 1. Explain the prefatory parts of a proposal in your own words.
2. Explain the four parts of the Introduction and the two parts of the Technical Procedure.
3. What do the Managerial Procedure and the Cost Estimate contain? What are contingencies?
4. Describe a small proposal idea of your own using your teacher’s format.
After recording: send the video in the group with “Day 21” in your message, then do your self-analysis
(mandatory).

days.title: Persuasive Communication & Hook Statements
days.content:
MYTH English Initiative | Phase 3 | Unit 2 and 3 | Page 56
DAY 23 | THURSDAY
WEEK 4
Pitching an Idea (Part 2): Process and Preparation, Six
Steps
Source: Pitching an Idea: Process, Preparation & Structure (slides 6 to 8)
1. READ
about 15 minutes
2. RECORD
about 15 minutes (speak 2 to 10 min)
3. SEND + SELF-ANALYSIS
mandatory
OFFICIAL STUDY MATERIAL (as given in your lecture slides / sample files)
Process & Preparation: Step 1 & 2: Attention and Interest Statements
 • Start with a Problem or Story. Begin by highlighting a customer problem or need. Create an emotional
connection. Use a rhetorical question or anecdote.
• Value Proposition. Craft a 1-2 sentence statement that clearly defines why your offering is the best
choice. Focus on uniqueness and benefits.
Process & Preparation: Step 3 & 4: Your Slides
 • Presenting with a Pitch Deck or Demo. Key points: use a slide deck (a parallel PPT on the thumbnail)
to visually support your pitch. Include relevant images, diagrams, and key points. Practice your script
thoroughly.
• Using Proof Points and Successes. Back up with data, testimonials, and case studies. This evidence
enhances credibility and persuades logically.
Process & Preparation: Step 5 & 6: Body Codes
 • Mastering Stage Presence. Use effective body language, maintain eye contact, and express genuine
enthusiasm. Your physical presence can greatly impact your pitch’s effectiveness.
• Closing with a Call to Action (CTA). End your pitch with a clear, actionable step for your audience.
This can include asking for investment, a meeting, or further discussion.
TEACHER’S EXPLANATION (to understand the topic deeply)
The six steps as one journey
 Step
What you do
Goal
1. Attention
Start with a problem or story
Make the listener want to listen
2. Interest
State your value proposition
Show why your idea is the best choice
3. Slides
Use a pitch deck or demo
Support your words with visuals
4. Proof
Use data, testimonials, case studies
Build trust and logic
5. Stage presence
Body language, eye contact, enthusiasm
Show confidence and honesty
6. Call to Action
Ask for a clear next step
Get a result
Step 1: Attention (start with a problem or story)
The first few seconds decide whether people listen. So do not start with ‘Good morning, today I will talk
about…’. Start with a customer problem or a small story, and create an emotional connection. A
rhetorical question (a question asked only to make people think, not to get an answer) or an anecdote (a
short real story) is a good beginning.

---
MYTH English Initiative | Phase 3 | Unit 2 and 3 | Page 57
Example: “Have you ever missed a last date because you did not know about it?” (A rhetorical question
that connects with student listeners.)
Step 2: Interest (value proposition)
A value proposition is a one or two sentence promise: what you offer and why it is better. Focus on
uniqueness and benefits, not on technical details. If the listener cannot repeat your value proposition after
the pitch, it is not clear enough.
EXTRA (not in the slides): A simple formula for writing a value proposition: “For [who has this problem],
our [idea] gives [main benefit], unlike [existing options].”
Step 3: Slides (pitch deck or demo)
A pitch deck is a short slide presentation, and a demo is a live show of your product. Visuals help people
understand and remember. Use relevant images, diagrams and only key points, and practise the script
thoroughly. The slide says the PPT runs parallel to your talk, meaning that it supports your speech and
does not replace it. Do not read from the slides.
Step 4: Proof points and successes
A good idea needs evidence. Use data (numbers), testimonials (words of satisfied users) and case
studies (real examples of success). Evidence increases credibility and persuades the listener logically, not
only emotionally.
Step 5: Stage presence (‘body codes’)
Your body also speaks. Use effective body language, maintain eye contact and show genuine enthusiasm.
You studied these in non-verbal communication in Unit 1. If you do not look excited about your own idea,
nobody else will be.
Step 6: Closing with a Call to Action (CTA)
End with a clear, actionable step: ‘Please give us a meeting next week’, ‘Invest in our prototype’, ‘Join our
pilot’. A pitch without a call to action leaves the audience with no direction.
EXAM TIP: Exam tip: write the six steps in order with one line for each. A quick way to remember them:
Attention, Interest, Slides, Proof, Presence, Call to Action.
VIDEO TASK: DAY 23
Speak for 2 to 10 minutes in your own words (do not read aloud). Cover these points:
 1. Explain the six steps of preparing a pitch in order.
2. What is a value proposition? Make one for an idea of your own.
3. Why do we need proof points? Name the three kinds of proof.
4. Give an opening line (a problem, a story or a rhetorical question) and a call to action for your idea.
After recording: send the video in the group with “Day 23” in your message, then do your self-analysis
(mandatory).

Pitch and Examples
Source: Pitching an Idea (slide 9) and Examples of Successful Idea Pitch given by your teacher

OFFICIAL STUDY MATERIAL (as given in your lecture slides / sample files)
Structure of a Successful Idea Pitch
 Structure of a Successful Idea Pitch (lecture slide)
• Hook: Start with a compelling opening that grabs your audience’s attention.
• Problem Statement: Clearly define the problem or opportunity your idea addresses.
• Solution: Present your idea as the ideal solution, showcasing its unique benefits.
• Evidence: Provide evidence and examples to back up the feasibility and potential success of your idea.
• Call to Action: End with a strong call to action, encouraging your audience to take the next steps.
Example 1: Lumina (a smart, energy-efficient home lighting system; a hypothetical
product)
Hook: “Imagine coming home to a house that responds to your mood, saves energy, and ensures your
safety, all while providing the perfect ambiance for any occasion.”
Problem Statement: “In today’s fast-paced world, energy consumption is at an all-time high, contributing
to expensive utility bills and environmental degradation. Additionally, conventional home lighting fails to
adapt to our personal needs and schedules, leading to wasted energy and compromised comfort.”
Solution: “Lumina is the solution: an intelligent, energy-efficient home lighting system that adapts to your
lifestyle. Using AI and smart sensors, Lumina adjusts the lighting based on the time of day, presence in the
room, and even your mood. Whether you’re hosting a party, working from home, or winding down for the
night, Lumina provides the perfect lighting settings to enhance your environment, all while saving up to 50%
on your energy bills.”

days.title: Technical Illustrations, Audience Analysis & Final Summary
days.content:
MYTH English Initiative | Phase 3 | Unit 2 and 3 | Page 62
DAY 25 | SATURDAY
WEEK 4
Elements of Speech Delivery: Passion, Poise and
Illustrations
Source: Elements of Speech Delivery lecture
1. READ
about 15 minutes
2. RECORD
about 15 minutes (speak 2 to 10 min)
3. SEND + SELF-ANALYSIS
mandatory
OFFICIAL STUDY MATERIAL (as given in your lecture slides / sample files)
Elements of effective, corporate speech delivery
 Elements of effective corporate speech delivery (lecture slide)
Passion
 • Passion is the strong belief in your content, that it will add value to your audience in a way.
• This belief makes one creatively work through different variables like audience reaction, technical
disruptions to make a complete presentation.
• This belief also helps you customize the case-studies, examples, Q&As, etc.
Poise
Poise is about keeping calm and in control while under fire or under pressure. For having poise:
 • a. Be focused on the audience’s needs: how your speech-inputs add value to their business or life.
• b. Adapt fast: have a mental preparation to change strategy vis-à-vis your audience. They could be: i.
Friendly, ii. Apathetic, iii. Hostile.
Poise for 3 types of audience
 • i. Friendly: They cooperate with you. So, add more customized examples. Plan small Q&A sessions.
• ii. Apathetic: They judge your ideas vis-à-vis other competitors. Provide balanced information, i.e. both
pros and cons. Your target is to give a subtle hint to why your ideas work better.
• iii. Hostile: They resist accepting your ideas. Agree with your audience’s viewpoint. Make them believe
you also agreed with their idea, until you came across a situation / data that changed your view. Also,
keep your presentation short, as the time-window of attention is lean.

---
MYTH English Initiative | Phase 3 | Unit 2 and 3 | Page 64
Audience
Meaning
What you should do (from the slide)
Friendly
They cooperate with you
Add more customized examples; plan small Q&A
sessions.
Apathetic
They are not excited; they compare
your ideas with competitors
Give balanced information (both pros and cons); give a
subtle hint about why your idea works better.
Hostile
They resist your ideas
Agree with their viewpoint; show that you also once
thought like them until some situation or data changed
your view; keep the presentation short.
Understanding the hostile audience: The idea is to start from common ground instead of starting a
fight. You respect their viewpoint, explain that you also had the same opinion earlier, and then show the
new fact or data that changed your mind. The listeners then follow the same path with you. Always be
truthful: use only a real change of view, never a pretended one. Keep the talk short, because the time for
which a hostile audience is willing to listen is limited.
4. Illustrations: make ideas easy to understand
 • Customize examples: The same concept needs different examples for school children, college
students and company managers. Choose examples according to the audience’s age, education and
socio-economic background so that they can digest the idea at their level of understanding.
• Use infographics: Choose the picture that fits the data. A pie chart is good to show the share of
different businesses in a market. Bar graphs are good to compare two trends over the years.
Example: Market share of five restaurants in a city: use a pie chart. Number of burgers and pizzas sold in
each month: use a bar graph.
EXAM TIP: Exam tip: write the three elements as headings, give the definition of passion and poise in
your own words, make the table of three audiences, and end with the two kinds of illustrations. Link it to
Unit 1 (non-verbal communication, 7 C’s) for extra marks.
VIDEO TASK: DAY 25
Speak for 2 to 10 minutes in your own words (do not read aloud). Cover these points:
 1. Explain the three elements of effective speech delivery.
2. What is poise? How will you behave with a friendly, an apathetic and a hostile audience?
3. Why do we customize examples? Give one example of customizing for school students and one for
company managers.
4. Which chart would you use for market share and which for comparing two trends? Why?
After recording: send the video in the group with “Day 25” in your message, then do your self-analysis
(mandatory).
